Examples are histone modifications around exons and within the gene body (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009; Schor et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Saint-André et al., 2011; Schor et al., 2013), nucleosome occupancy (Schwartz et al., 2009; Tilgner et al., 2009), GC content of both intronic and exonic DNA (Schwartz et al., 2009; Amit et al., 2012), and DNA methylation (Maunakea et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to relevant studies.

claims.claim: Nucleosome occupancy is associated with exons.
claims.source: Genic features that could potentially influence elongation rates are often, but not exclusively, associated with exons. Examples are histone modifications around exons and within the gene body (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009; Schor et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Saint-André et al., 2011; Schor et al., 2013), nucleosome occupancy (Schwartz et al., 2009; Tilgner et al., 2009), GC content of both intronic and exonic DNA (Schwartz et al., 2009; Amit et al., 2012), and DNA methylation (Maunakea et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2009 and Tilgner et al., 2009.

claims.claim: GC content of both intronic and exonic DNA is associated with exons.
claims.source: Genic features that could potentially influence elongation rates are often, but not exclusively, associated with exons. Examples are histone modifications around exons and within the gene body (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009; Schor et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Saint-André et al., 2011; Schor et al., 2013), nucleosome occupancy (Schwartz et al., 2009; Tilgner et al., 2009), GC content of both intronic and exonic DNA (Schwartz et al., 2009; Amit et al., 2012), and DNA methylation (Maunakea et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2009 and Amit et al., 2012.

claims.claim: DNA methylation is associated with exons.
claims.source: Genic features that could potentially influence elongation rates are often, but not exclusively, associated with exons. Examples are histone modifications around exons and within the gene body (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009; Schor et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Saint-André et al., 2011; Schor et al., 2013), nucleosome occupancy (Schwartz et al., 2009; Tilgner et al., 2009), GC content of both intronic and exonic DNA (Schwartz et al., 2009; Amit et al., 2012), and DNA methylation (Maunakea et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Maunakea et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Many exonic chromatin features have been implicated in regulation of splicing.
claims.source: Many exonic chromatin features have been implicated in regulation of splicing as well (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009; Schor et al., 2009; Shukla et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Pol II accumulates preferentially at spliced exons.
claims.source: Moreover, Pol II has been shown to accumulate preferentially at spliced exons (Brodsky et al., 2005; Alexander et al., 2010; Chodavarapu et al., 2010; Kwak et al., 2013), leading to the hypothesis that reduction of Pol II elongation rate facilitates splice site recognition and spliceosome assembly, and thus, splicing of the associated intron (Shukla and Oberdoerffer, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Reduction of Pol II elongation rate facilitates splice site recognition and spliceosome assembly.
claims.source: Moreover, Pol II has been shown to accumulate preferentially at spliced exons (Brodsky et al., 2005; Alexander et al., 2010; Chodavarapu et al., 2010; Kwak et al., 2013), leading to the hypothesis that reduction of Pol II elongation rate facilitates splice site recognition and spliceosome assembly, and thus, splicing of the associated intron (Shukla and Oberdoerffer, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations of Pol II accumulation at exons.

claims.claim: Transcription with a slow mutant of Pol II promotes alternative splicing in human and yeast cells.
claims.source: Indeed, transcription with a slow mutant of Pol II promotes alternative splicing in human and yeast cells (Howe et al., 2003; de la Mata et al., 2003; de la Mata et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Three studies that directly measured elongation rates at multiple genes could not clearly demonstrate a correlation between exons and elongation rate.
claims.source: Despite observations of Pol II accumulation at exons, three studies that directly measured elongation rates at multiple genes could not clearly demonstrate a correlation between exons and elongation rate (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Brody et al., 2011; Danko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to three studies.

claims.claim: In vitro studies clearly show the effect of nucleosomes and histone modifications on elongation rate.
claims.source: Furthermore, although in vitro studies clearly show the effect of nucleosomes and histone modifications on elongation rate (Orphanides et al., 1998; Hodges et al., 2009; Bintu et al., 2012), the in vivo consequences of chromatin on elongation rate are less understood, primarily because of the inability to measure elongation rates at many genes simultaneously.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claims.claim: Previous studies have measured elongation rates ranging from 1 to 4 kb/min at individual genes in various organisms.
claims.source: Previous studies have measured elongation rates ranging from 1 to 4 kb/min at individual genes in various organisms (Ardehali and Lis, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claims.claim: Elongation rates for over 160 genes were measured simultaneously by following the induction wave of Pol II after estradiol or TNF-alpha treatment.
claims.source: Recently, elongation rates for over 160 genes were measured simultaneously by following the induction wave of Pol II after estradiol or TNF-alpha treatment (Danko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Danko et al., 2013.

claims.claim: A broad range of elongation rates occurs between and within cell types.
claims.source: Interestingly, this study showed a broad range of elongation rates between and within cell types, suggesting that the control of elongation rate may be used to regulate transcription and co-transcriptional processes.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Danko et al., 2013.

claims.claim: 300 nM Flavopiridol was used to block pause escape in mES cells.
claims.source: We isolated replicates of nuclei from untreated mESCs and cells treated for 2, 5, 12.5, 25 and 50 min with 300 nM FP, as well as nuclei treated for 12.5, 25, and 50 min with 500 nM Trp (Figure 1A) and performed GRO-seq with these nuclei (Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Experimental design described in methods.

claims.claim: 500 nM Triptolide was used to block transcription initiation in mES cells.
claims.source: We isolated replicates of nuclei from untreated mESCs and cells treated for 2, 5, 12.5, 25 and 50 min with 300 nM FP, as well as nuclei treated for 12.5, 25, and 50 min with 500 nM Trp (Figure 1A) and performed GRO-seq with these nuclei (Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Experimental design described in methods.

claims.claim: Biological replicates of GRO-seq experiments correlated extremely well.
claims.source: Biological replicates correlated extremely well (Figure 1—source data 2 and 3) and were combined for further analysis.
claims.evidence: Stated in methods with reference to source data.

claims.claim: Treated and control GRO-seq libraries were normalized to in vitro transcribed Arabidopsis thaliana RNAs added during the run-on.
claims.source: Because inhibition of P-TEFb and initiation were anticipated to have large genome-wide effects on Pol II transcription, we normalized treated and control libraries to in vitro transcribed Arabidopsis thaliana RNAs added during the run-on.
claims.evidence: Normalization method described in results.

claims.claim: FP treatment causes an overall ~50% reduction of phosphorylation of bound Pol II at both Ser2 and Ser5.
claims.source: FP treatment causes an overall ∼50% reduction of phosphorylation of bound Pol II at both Ser2 and Ser5.
claims.evidence: Shown by western blot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: After FP or Trp treatment the bound fraction of total Pol II was reduced to ~50 and 30%, respectively.
claims.source: After FP or Trp treatment the bound fraction of total Pol II was reduced to ∼50 and 30%, respectively, while the free fraction was increased after treatment with FP, but not with Trp.
claims.evidence: Shown by western blot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The free fraction of Pol II was increased after treatment with FP, but not with Trp.
claims.source: After FP or Trp treatment the bound fraction of total Pol II was reduced to ∼50 and 30%, respectively, while the free fraction was increased after treatment with FP, but not with Trp.
claims.evidence: Shown by western blot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Both FP and Trp work rapidly, as gene body density near the TSS approaches background levels within 12.5 min.
claims.source: Both drugs work rapidly, as gene body density near the TSS approaches background levels within 12.5 min.
claims.evidence: Observed in composite profiles and individual gene examples.

claims.claim: Elongating Pol II in the gene body is not affected by FP or Trp treatment downstream of the inhibition waves.
claims.source: Downstream of these inhibition waves, Pol II density levels remain equal throughout the time course, indicating that elongating Pol II in the gene body is not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: Trp blocks transcription initiation and causes the time dependent clearing of Pol II from the promoter and gene body.
claims.source: These results confirm that Trp blocks transcription initiation and causes the time dependent clearing of Pol II from the promoter and gene body, while FP's prominent effect is to block escape from the pause, causing a time dependent gene body clearance but enhanced promoter proximal Pol II pausing.
claims.evidence: Observed in GRO-seq data after drug treatment.

claims.claim: FP's prominent effect is to block escape from the pause, causing a time dependent gene body clearance but enhanced promoter proximal Pol II pausing.
claims.source: These results confirm that Trp blocks transcription initiation and causes the time dependent clearing of Pol II from the promoter and gene body, while FP's prominent effect is to block escape from the pause, causing a time dependent gene body clearance but enhanced promoter proximal Pol II pausing.
claims.evidence: Observed in GRO-seq data after drug treatment.

claims.claim: 96% of genes are significantly decreased after Trp treatment.
claims.source: Quantification of the decrease in read density directly downstream of the TSS shows that 96% of genes are significantly decreased after Trp treatment, while 95% of genes are decreased after FP treatment (Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Quantified from GRO-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 95% of genes are decreased after FP treatment.
claims.source: Quantification of the decrease in read density directly downstream of the TSS shows that 96% of genes are significantly decreased after Trp treatment, while 95% of genes are decreased after FP treatment (Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Quantified from GRO-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: P-TEFb-dependent Pol II entry into productive elongation is as universal a step in gene transcription as TFIIH helicase-dependent initiation.
claims.source: This demonstrates that P-TEFb-dependent Pol II entry into productive elongation is as universal a step in gene transcription as TFIIH helicase-dependent initiation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that both FP and Trp affect >95% of genes.

claims.claim: The mean half-life of paused Pol II is 6.9 min.
claims.source: The mean half-life of Pol II is 6.9 min, in agreement with the decay rates measured in Drosophila (Henriques et al., 2013; Buckley et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Calculated from decay rate measurements after Trp treatment.

claims.claim: Promoter proximal Pol II stability is comparable between species.
claims.source: Thus, promoter proximal Pol II stability is comparable between species and paused Pol II is relatively stable.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of measured half-lives in mES cells with published Drosophila data.

claims.claim: The Trp inhibition wave was less clearly defined than the FP wave.
claims.source: The Trp inhibition wave was less clearly defined than the FP wave, likely due to the fact that Pol II initiated and paused before Trp treatment will gradually escape after TFIIH inhibition, resulting in a less defined block of Pol II entry into the gene body (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, see Med13l).
claims.evidence: Observed in GRO-seq data and HMM analysis.

claims.claim: On average, Pol II travels about 100 kb during 50 min of FP treatment.
claims.source: On average, Pol II travels about 100 kb during 50 min of FP treatment.
claims.evidence: Calculated from HMM-derived transition points.

claims.claim: The average Pol II inhibition wave travels at identical rates after either Trp or FP treatment.
claims.source: The average Pol II inhibition wave travels at identical rates after either Trp or FP treatment, indicating that inhibition of P-TEFb or off-target effects of FP are unlikely to have significant effects on elongation rates downstream of the promoter proximal region (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Shown by comparison of transition points in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: 141 early elongation rates (5-12.5 min) were measured with an average of 0.5 kb/min.
claims.source: We directly measured 141 early (5–12.5 min), 938 mid (12.5–25 min), and 245 late (25-50 min) elongation rates, with average elongation rates of 0.5, 1.8 and 2.4 kb/min respectively (Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Calculated from HMM-derived transition points.

claims.claim: 938 mid elongation rates (12.5-25 min) were measured with an average of 1.8 kb/min.
claims.source: We directly measured 141 early (5–12.5 min), 938 mid (12.5–25 min), and 245 late (25-50 min) elongation rates, with average elongation rates of 0.5, 1.8 and 2.4 kb/min respectively (Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Calculated from HMM-derived transition points.

claims.claim: 245 late elongation rates (25-50 min) were measured with an average of 2.4 kb/min.
claims.source: We directly measured 141 early (5–12.5 min), 938 mid (12.5–25 min), and 245 late (25-50 min) elongation rates, with average elongation rates of 0.5, 1.8 and 2.4 kb/min respectively (Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Calculated from HMM-derived transition points.

claims.claim: The slope of the intronic density plots decreases as the directly measured elongation rates become faster.
claims.source: The slope of the intronic density plots of the quartiles decreases as the directly measured elongation rates become faster (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, right), independently confirming the gene-to-gene variation in elongation rates.
claims.evidence: Shown by RNA-seq intronic gradient analysis in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The slope of intron read density as a function of distance to the 3′ SS is higher in the upstream region compared to the downstream region within the same genes.
claims.source: The slope of intron read density as a function of distance to the 3′ SS is higher in the upstream region compared to the downstream region (Figure 3F), indicative of slower elongation rates upstream in genes, and acceleration as Pol II travels within the gene body.
claims.evidence: Shown by RNA-seq intronic gradient analysis in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The acceleration of Pol II is not constant, but decreases as transcription proceeds.
claims.source: The acceleration is not constant, but decreases as transcription proceeds (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C), suggesting that the Pol II elongation complex 'matures' and reaches its maximum speed while transcribing a gene.
claims.evidence: Shown by analysis of acceleration constants in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C.

claims.claim: Pausing negatively correlates with mid elongation rates.
claims.source: Indeed, pausing negatively correlates with mid elongation rates, while late elongation rates are not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), suggesting that pausing delays the maturation of Pol II.
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: Late elongation rates are not affected by pausing.
claims.source: Indeed, pausing negatively correlates with mid elongation rates, while late elongation rates are not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), suggesting that pausing delays the maturation of Pol II.
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: Pol II Ser2 phosphorylation increases gradually within the gene body within the same region as the acceleration of the elongation complex.
claims.source: Furthermore, ChIP-seq composite profiles of total Pol II and of Ser5 or Ser2 phosphorylated CTD (Rahl et al., 2010) show that Pol II Ser2 phosphorylation, which is a product of P-TEFb activity and other kinases (Bartkowiak et al., 2010; Devaiah et al., 2012) and presumably coincides with the loss of NELF and DSIF pausing activity, increases gradually within the gene body within the same region as the acceleration of the elongation complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E,F).
claims.evidence: Shown by ChIP-seq analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E,F.

claims.claim: Pol II Ser2 phosphorylation is a product of P-TEFb activity and other kinases.
claims.source: Furthermore, ChIP-seq composite profiles of total Pol II and of Ser5 or Ser2 phosphorylated CTD (Rahl et al., 2010) show that Pol II Ser2 phosphorylation, which is a product of P-TEFb activity and other kinases (Bartkowiak et al., 2010; Devaiah et al., 2012) and presumably coincides with the loss of NELF and DSIF pausing activity, increases gradually within the gene body within the same region as the acceleration of the elongation complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bartkowiak et al., 2010 and Devaiah et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The inverse of the elongation rate does not fall below the density plot in the gene body region where the rates are measured.
claims.source: On average, the inverse of the elongation rate (v−1) does not fall below the density plot (D) in the gene body region (Figure 4B) where the rates are measured (starting from the average 5 min transition point 2.3 kb downstream of TSS).
claims.evidence: Shown by comparison of v−1 and D in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The bulk of the change in Pol II density stems from the acceleration of stably elongating Pol II molecules.
claims.source: This indicates that the bulk of the change in Pol II density stems from the acceleration of stably elongating Pol II molecules.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the relationship between v−1 and D, and supported by simulation analysis.

claims.claim: Pol II termination does not appear to have a global contribution to the amount of Pol II in the regions more downstream of 2–3 kb from the TSS.
claims.source: Therefore, Pol II termination does not appear to have a global contribution to the amount of Pol II in the regions more downstream of 2–3 kb from the TSS.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of measured data with simulated models.

claims.claim: Genes that are relatively highly expressed show a log-log slope of 1.8 between mRNA level and GRO-seq density.
claims.source: Interestingly, genes that are relatively highly expressed show a slope of 1.8 indicating that mRNA level is not a simple function of GRO-seq density for these genes (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: There is a modest correlation between elongation rate and GRO-seq density.
claims.source: We observed a modest correlation between elongation rate and GRO-seq (Figure 4F), indicating that highly active genes have faster elongation rates and produce more mRNA, in agreement with a previous analysis of a smaller set of inducible genes (Danko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Highly active genes have faster elongation rates and produce more mRNA.
claims.source: We observed a modest correlation between elongation rate and GRO-seq (Figure 4F), indicating that highly active genes have faster elongation rates and produce more mRNA, in agreement with a previous analysis of a smaller set of inducible genes (Danko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Inferred from correlation between elongation rate and GRO-seq density.

claims.claim: Highly expressed genes display a log-log slope of 2.2 between mRNA-seq and GRO-seq.
claims.source: These highly expressed genes display a log–log slope of 2.2 (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: When plotting production rates vs mRNA level, the slope is reduced to 1.6.
claims.source: In contrast, when plotting the production rates, that is the mid elongation rates multiplied by the corresponding GRO-seq densities, vs mRNA level, the slope is reduced to 1.6 (Figure 4H), indicating that elongation rate can partially explain the divergence between Pol II density and the mRNA level at highly transcribed genes.
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Elongation rate can partially explain the divergence between Pol II density and the mRNA level at highly transcribed genes.
claims.source: In contrast, when plotting the production rates, that is the mid elongation rates multiplied by the corresponding GRO-seq densities, vs mRNA level, the slope is reduced to 1.6 (Figure 4H), indicating that elongation rate can partially explain the divergence between Pol II density and the mRNA level at highly transcribed genes.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the reduction in slope when accounting for elongation rates.

claims.claim: H3K36me3 and CpG methylation were depleted over larger regions around the TSS in faster genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, H3K36me3 and CpG methylation were depleted over larger regions around the TSS in faster genes, while H3K4me1 and H3K79me2 were enriched in these same regions (Figure 5A, right).
claims.evidence: Shown by ChIP-seq density profiles in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: H3K4me1 and H3K79me2 were enriched in regions around the TSS in faster genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, H3K36me3 and CpG methylation were depleted over larger regions around the TSS in faster genes, while H3K4me1 and H3K79me2 were enriched in these same regions (Figure 5A, right).
claims.evidence: Shown by ChIP-seq density profiles in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: CpG methylation and H3K36me3 are enriched at exons.
claims.source: CpG methylation and H3K36me3 are enriched at exons, while H3K79me2 levels decrease upon encountering the second exon (Schwartz et al., 2009; Huff et al., 2010; Maunakea et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: H3K79me2 levels decrease upon encountering the second exon.
claims.source: CpG methylation and H3K36me3 are enriched at exons, while H3K79me2 levels decrease upon encountering the second exon (Schwartz et al., 2009; Huff et al., 2010; Maunakea et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The elongation complex tends to travel faster in genes with larger first introns.
claims.source: Therefore, we examined the correlation between elongation rate and the length of intron 1 (Figure 5A). Indeed, the elongation complex tends to travel faster in genes with larger first introns.
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Addition of an exon within the early elongation rate region results in an average delay of 37 seconds.
claims.source: Addition of an exon within the three regions, in which early, mid, and late elongation rates were derived, results in average delays of 37, 31 or 23 s respectively.
claims.evidence: Calculated from linear regression of exon density vs elongation rate.

claims.claim: Addition of an exon within the mid elongation rate region results in an average delay of 31 seconds.
claims.source: Addition of an exon within the three regions, in which early, mid, and late elongation rates were derived, results in average delays of 37, 31 or 23 s respectively.
claims.evidence: Calculated from linear regression of exon density vs elongation rate.

claims.claim: Addition of an exon within the late elongation rate region results in an average delay of 23 seconds.
claims.source: Addition of an exon within the three regions, in which early, mid, and late elongation rates were derived, results in average delays of 37, 31 or 23 s respectively.
claims.evidence: Calculated from linear regression of exon density vs elongation rate.

claims.claim: The delay at exons is somewhat less in downstream regions of the gene body when Pol II is more fully phosphorylated.
claims.source: Thus, the co-transcriptional delay of Pol II at exons is striking and might be linked to coupled splicing events. Interestingly, the delay is somewhat less in downstream regions of the gene body when Pol II is more fully phosphorylated (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F) and is generally elongating faster (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of delays at different regions and correlation with Pol II phosphorylation.

claims.claim: There is a striking positive correlation between CG content at promoters (CpG islands) and downstream mid elongation rates.
claims.source: We found a striking positive correlation between CG content at promoters, that is CpG islands, and the downstream mid elongation rates (Figure 5C, left).
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Unmethylated CpG islands are often associated with broad transcription initiation.
claims.source: Unmethylated CpG islands are often associated with broad transcription initiation (Core et al., 2008), likely because CpG islands deter nucleosome binding (Ramirez-Carrozzi et al., 2009; Fenouil et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: CpG islands deter nucleosome binding.
claims.source: Unmethylated CpG islands are often associated with broad transcription initiation (Core et al., 2008), likely because CpG islands deter nucleosome binding (Ramirez-Carrozzi et al., 2009; Fenouil et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Nucleosomes can be barriers to Pol II elongation and cause transient pauses to delay the Pol II traversal.
claims.source: Interestingly, nucleosomes can be barriers to Pol II elongation and cause transient pauses to delay the Pol II traversal (Hodges et al., 2009; Bintu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The nucleosome free region (NFR) is wider in genes with faster elongation rates.
claims.source: Therefore we explored the nucleosome occupancy as a function of elongation rates, and found that the nucleosome free region (NFR) is wider in genes with faster elongation rates (Figure 5C, right); the fastest gene group is shifted approximately 2 nucleosomes downstream compared to the slowest genes.
claims.evidence: Shown by nucleosome occupancy analysis in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The fastest gene group is shifted approximately 2 nucleosomes downstream compared to the slowest genes.
claims.source: Therefore we explored the nucleosome occupancy as a function of elongation rates, and found that the nucleosome free region (NFR) is wider in genes with faster elongation rates (Figure 5C, right); the fastest gene group is shifted approximately 2 nucleosomes downstream compared to the slowest genes.
claims.evidence: Shown by nucleosome occupancy analysis in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: A more nucleosome-free promoter architecture correlates positively with elongation rates.
claims.source: This shows that a more nucleosome-free promoter architecture correlates positively with elongation rates, and implicates an intrinsic component of Pol II rate is determined in the earliest stages of transcription.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the correlation between NFR width and elongation rates.

claims.claim: The top 20 6-mer sequences associated with slower elongation rates were enriched for repeats of CG dinucleotides.
claims.source: Interestingly, the top 20 6-mer sequences associated with slower elongation rates were enriched for repeats of CG dinucleotides (Figure 5D, left).
claims.evidence: Shown by 6-mer sequence analysis in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: There is a modest negative correlation between CG density and elongation rates in individual genes.
claims.source: Moreover, we found a modest negative correlation between the CG density and the elongation rates in individual genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), opposite of the effect CG content has at the promoter.
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Elongation rate is positively related to the NFR and GC content at promoters.
claims.source: Interestingly, while elongation rates seems to be positively related to the NFR and GC content at promoters, elongation rate correlates negatively with CG content within the gene body (Figure 5D, right panel) and is unaffected by nucleosome occupancy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analyses in Figure 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: Elongation rate correlates negatively with CG content within the gene body.
claims.source: Interestingly, while elongation rates seems to be positively related to the NFR and GC content at promoters, elongation rate correlates negatively with CG content within the gene body (Figure 5D, right panel) and is unaffected by nucleosome occupancy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Elongation rate is unaffected by nucleosome occupancy in the gene body.
claims.source: Interestingly, while elongation rates seems to be positively related to the NFR and GC content at promoters, elongation rate correlates negatively with CG content within the gene body (Figure 5D, right panel) and is unaffected by nucleosome occupancy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Shown by analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The negative effect of CG content on elongation rate is independent of exonic enrichment for CG content and nucleosomes.
claims.source: This negative effect also seems independent of exonic enrichment for CG content and nucleosomes (Schwartz et al., 2009; Tilgner et al., 2009), as we still observed the correlation between elongation rates and CG content in intronic regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Shown by analysis of intronic CG content in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The increased melting temperature of GC-rich DNA may explain the general reduction of elongation rates.
claims.source: The increased melting temperature of GC-rich DNA may explain this general reduction of elongation rates (Nechaev et al., 2010), but the methylation status of the CG dinucleotides (Figure 5A) may also lead to differential regulation of Pol II elongation rates.
claims.evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation.

claims.claim: The methylation status of CG dinucleotides may lead to differential regulation of Pol II elongation rates.
claims.source: The increased melting temperature of GC-rich DNA may explain this general reduction of elongation rates (Nechaev et al., 2010), but the methylation status of the CG dinucleotides (Figure 5A) may also lead to differential regulation of Pol II elongation rates.
claims.evidence: Speculative explanation based on observed correlations.

claims.claim: Exon density has the strongest correlation with elongation rates among all examined features.
claims.source: All of these features are significantly associated with the elongation rates, the exon density having the strongest correlation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Shown by multivariate regression analysis in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The correlation between elongation rates and intron 1 length can be explained almost entirely by exon density alone.
claims.source: For example, the correlation between elongation rates and intron 1 length, gene body H3K36me3, and H3K4me1 can be explained almost entirely by the exon density alone (Figure 6B), since they do not show correlation with the residual of the elongation rates after fitting to the exon density model (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Shown by iterative regression analysis in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Gene body H3K79me2 and gene body CpG features cannot be explained mostly by exon density.
claims.source: However, gene body H3K79me2 and gene body CpG features cannot be explained mostly by exon density (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Shown by iterative regression analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: H3K79me2 and CpG content have independent components from each other.
claims.source: Likewise, H3K79me2 and CpG content have independent components from each other, while CpG methylation is tightly associated with CpG content (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Shown by iterative regression analysis in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: CpG methylation is tightly associated with CpG content.
claims.source: Likewise, H3K79me2 and CpG content have independent components from each other, while CpG methylation is tightly associated with CpG content (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Shown by iterative regression analysis in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: CpG content, exon density, and H3K79me2 are the main modulators of elongation rate.

results.result: Both Flavopiridol (FP) and Triptolide (Trp) block transcription at more than 95% of genes in mouse ES cells, demonstrating that P-TEFb-dependent pause escape is as universal as TFIIH-dependent initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C50, C51 provide quantitative GRO-seq data showing 96% of genes decreased after Trp and 95% after FP treatment. C2 and C52 appropriately infer from this data that pause escape is a ubiquitous step in transcription. The experimental design with appropriate controls and normalization (C39-C42) supports these conclusions.

results.result: Paused Pol II has a mean half-life of approximately 7 minutes at ~3200 genes, indicating remarkable stability and ruling out rapid termination-reinitiation cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C53, and C110 consistently report a ~7 min half-life calculated from decay rates after Trp treatment using exponential decay modeling. C54 appropriately compares this to Drosophila data. C111's inference that this stability excludes rapid termination cycles is reasonable given the relatively long half-life.

results.result: Pol II elongation rates were measured at over 1000 genes using a Hidden Markov Model to track inhibition waves, yielding rates of 0.5 kb/min (early), 1.8 kb/min (mid), and 2.4 kb/min (late).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 provide specific numbers of measurements (141 early, 938 mid, 245 late) with corresponding average rates. The HMM methodology is described and validated through multiple approaches (C55-C57, C61-C62). Independent confirmation using RNA-seq intronic gradients (C61-C62) strengthens confidence in the measurements.

results.result: Pol II accelerates dramatically as it transcribes through genes, with rates increasing from 0.5 kb/min early to 2.4 kb/min late, and this acceleration decreases as transcription proceeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 show progressive increase in elongation rates. C62 provides independent validation through RNA-seq intronic gradients showing steeper slopes upstream vs downstream. C63 demonstrates that acceleration is not constant but decreases over distance. Multiple independent lines of evidence (direct measurement, RNA-seq gradients, within-gene comparisons) converge on this conclusion.

results.result: Pol II slows down at exons, with delays of 23-37 seconds per exon depending on gene position, and exon density is the strongest predictor of elongation rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 provide quantitative delays per exon from linear regression analysis. C101 establishes exon density as the strongest correlate among all features examined. C133 appropriately infers that Pol II slows at each exon based on the strong negative correlation. The delay decreasing in downstream regions (C85) is consistent with the acceleration model.

results.result: H3K79me2 has a positive effect on elongation rates, is enriched in the first exon and intron, and represents an independent predictor that cannot be explained by exon density alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C78 establish the positive correlation. C103 demonstrates through iterative regression that H3K79me2 effects are independent of exon density. C106 shows it's one of three main modulators in multivariate analysis. C107-C108 appropriately infer its role in early elongation based on its enrichment pattern. The statistical approach is sound.

results.result: CG content within genes has a negative effect on elongation rates, independent of exonic enrichment, with CG-rich 6-mers associated with slower rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 show enrichment of CG-rich sequences in slow genes. C96 and C98 demonstrate the effect persists in intronic regions, ruling out confounding by exonic features. C101 and C106 establish CG content as one of three main independent modulators through multivariate analysis. The evidence is consistent across multiple analytical approaches.

results.result: Approximately 30% of intergenic variation in elongation rates can be explained by three features: exon density, CpG content, and H3K79me2, which have independent effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 states the overall predictive power. Claims C101-C106 describe the multivariate regression analysis establishing independence of the three main factors. The iterative regression approach (C102-C105) appropriately tests for independence. The 30% explained variance is reasonable for biological data and represents a substantial advance in understanding elongation rate determinants.

results.result: Pausing negatively correlates with mid elongation rates but not late elongation rates, suggesting pausing delays Pol II maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 present correlation data showing differential effects on mid vs late rates. The inference that pausing delays maturation is reasonable given the acceleration model and the specific pattern of correlation. This is consistent with the broader model of Pol II maturation during elongation (C63, C66).

results.result: Pol II Ser2 phosphorylation increases gradually within the gene body in the same region as elongation complex acceleration, and is a product of P-TEFb and other kinases.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 presents ChIP-seq data showing gradual increase in Ser2 phosphorylation correlating with acceleration. C67 correctly attributes Ser2 phosphorylation to P-TEFb and other kinases based on established literature. The correlation between phosphorylation and acceleration supports the maturation model, though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: The bulk of change in Pol II density stems from acceleration of stably elongating molecules rather than termination, as the inverse elongation rate does not fall below the density plot.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 presents the key observation comparing v⁻¹ and D. C69 appropriately infers that acceleration rather than termination explains density changes. C70 concludes termination doesn't contribute globally beyond 2-3 kb from TSS. The simulation analysis described in methods and Figure 4 supplement provides additional support for distinguishing acceleration from termination models.

results.result: Elongation rate partially explains the divergence between Pol II density and mRNA levels at highly transcribed genes, reducing the log-log slope from 2.2 to 1.6 when production rates are considered.
results.evaluation: Claims C71 and C74 establish the non-linear relationship between GRO-seq and mRNA-seq. C72-C73 show correlation between elongation rate and transcription. C75-C76 demonstrate that accounting for elongation rate reduces but doesn't eliminate the slope deviation. The analysis appropriately acknowledges that other factors (mRNA stability, processing) likely contribute to the remaining correlation.

results.result: CG content at promoters (CpG islands) positively correlates with downstream elongation rates, associated with wider nucleosome-free regions that are shifted ~2 nucleosomes downstream in faster genes.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 establishes the positive correlation at promoters (opposite to gene body effects). C87-C88 provide mechanistic context linking CpG islands to nucleosome depletion. C90-C91 quantify the NFR differences between fast and slow genes. C92's inference that promoter architecture influences elongation rates is reasonable, though the mechanism connecting promoter structure to downstream elongation remains unclear.

results.result: The experimental approach using 300 nM FP and 500 nM Trp with GRO-seq produces rapid, specific effects on Pol II with minimal off-target effects, as evidenced by drug-specific changes in Pol II phosphorylation and distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 describe the experimental design with appropriate controls and normalization. C43-C45 show drug-specific effects on Pol II phosphorylation and chromatin binding consistent with known mechanisms. C46-C47 demonstrate rapid action with minimal effects on elongating Pol II downstream of inhibition waves. The biological replicates correlated well (C41), supporting reproducibility.

results.result: Trp blocks initiation causing time-dependent clearing of Pol II, while FP blocks pause escape causing gene body clearance but enhanced pausing, with remarkably similar inhibition profiles in gene bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 describe the distinct effects of each drug consistent with their known mechanisms. C123 notes the similar gene body profiles, supporting specificity of action. The visual data in Figures 1-2 clearly show the expected patterns. This validates the experimental approach and confirms the drugs work as intended with minimal off-target effects.

results.result: The Trp inhibition wave is less clearly defined than the FP wave, but average transition points travel at identical rates after either treatment.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 acknowledges a technical limitation with reasonable explanation (paused Pol II escaping after Trp treatment). C57 demonstrates that despite this, the measured rates are consistent between treatments, validating the approach. This strengthens confidence that the measurements reflect true elongation rates rather than drug-specific artifacts.

results.result: RNA-seq intronic gradients independently confirm gene-to-gene variation in elongation rates and acceleration within genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 describe independent validation using RNA-seq intronic read patterns. The method is based on sound reasoning about co-transcriptional splicing kinetics. The concordance between direct GRO-seq measurements and RNA-seq gradients strengthens confidence in both the elongation rate measurements and the acceleration model.

results.result: Not all active genes show promoter proximal Pol II accumulation, as accumulation depends on the balance between initiation rate, escape rate, and the activities of various transcription factors and pausing factors.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 presents the observation. C114 provides the logical framework for understanding pausing dynamics. C115-C116 cite literature showing different transcription factors have different effects on pausing and escape. The reasoning is sound and consistent with the kinetic model of pausing, though the specific factors determining accumulation at individual genes remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: A small fraction of poorly expressed, weakly paused genes show reduced paused Pol II after FP treatment, possibly due to feedback between pausing dynamics and initiation.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 presents an observation that contradicts the main model. C120 offers a speculative explanation involving feedback between pausing and initiation. C121 cites one example from literature. While the observation is noted, the explanation remains speculative and the mechanism is unclear. This represents an interesting exception that warrants further investigation but doesn't undermine the main conclusions.

results.result: Elongation rates after P-TEFb inhibition are slightly lower than rates after induction, possibly due to lagging Pol II pushing leading Pol II.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 notes a difference compared to published data. C125 offers a speculative mechanistic explanation. The comparison is confounded by different experimental approaches (inhibition vs induction) and potentially different cell types or conditions. The proposed mechanism is plausible but not tested. This represents an interesting hypothesis requiring further investigation.

results.result: DNA methylation levels and H3K79me2 effects on elongation rates could explain differences between mESC and differentiated cells, and H3K79me2 repression during reprogramming could work through elongation rate modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C128 cite literature on methylation levels and reprogramming. C127 and C129 offer speculative explanations connecting these observations to elongation rates. While the logic is reasonable, these are hypotheses rather than tested conclusions. The connections between elongation rates, gene expression, and cellular phenotypes remain to be directly demonstrated.

results.result: Variation in elongation rates can lead to differences of an hour or more in mRNA production timing, which could be relevant for development and stress responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 make reasonable calculations based on measured elongation rates and known gene lengths. C132 appropriately cites literature on the importance of timing in development and stress. While the functional significance of elongation rate variation for timing is not directly tested, the calculations are sound and the hypothesis is well-supported by the data and literature.

results.result: The observed slowdown at exons supports coupling between Pol II elongation rates and splicing at all exons, though effects on alternative splicing outcomes remain to be determined.
results.evaluation: Claim C134 offers a speculative mechanism for exon-associated slowing. C135 cites literature showing elongation affects splicing. C136 appropriately concludes that the data support coupling while acknowledging limitations in assessing alternative splicing outcomes. The conclusion is measured and appropriate given the data, which demonstrate correlation but not causation or specific effects on splicing patterns.

results.result: Background on P-TEFb, pausing mechanisms, and prior work in Drosophila and mammals establishing the regulatory importance of promoter-proximal pausing.
results.evaluation: These claims (C11-C21) summarize established knowledge from the literature with appropriate citations. They provide necessary context for the current work. The citations appear appropriate and the summaries are consistent with the cited work. This represents accurate reporting of prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Background on elongation rate effects on co-transcriptional processes, genomic features associated with elongation, and prior elongation rate measurements.
results.evaluation: These claims (C22-C38) summarize relevant prior work with appropriate citations. They establish the context for why measuring elongation rates at many genes simultaneously is important and what was previously known. The literature summary appears accurate and comprehensive. This represents appropriate contextualization of the current work.

results.result: Various chromatin marks show specific patterns relative to elongation rates and gene structure, with H3K36me3 and CpG methylation depleted in faster genes while H3K4me1 and H3K79me2 are enriched.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 present ChIP-seq correlation data. C79-C80 cite literature on chromatin mark distributions. C81 shows correlation between first intron length and elongation rate. The correlations are clearly demonstrated, though the mechanistic connections and causal relationships remain to be fully established. The data support the correlations but don't definitively establish mechanisms.

results.result: Elongation rate shows opposite correlations with CG content at promoters (positive) versus gene bodies (negative), and is unaffected by nucleosome occupancy in gene bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 establish the contrasting effects of CG content at different locations. C97 notes lack of correlation with gene body nucleosome occupancy. C98 shows the gene body CG effect is independent of exonic features. The observations are well-supported, though the mechanistic basis for the opposite effects at promoters vs gene bodies remains unclear.

results.result: The negative effect of GC-rich DNA on elongation rates may be explained by increased melting temperature or differential methylation status.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 offer speculative mechanistic explanations for the observed CG content effects. While the hypotheses are reasonable and C99 cites supporting literature, these remain untested explanations. The actual mechanism by which CG content affects elongation rates in vivo is not established by the data presented.

results.result: Correlations between elongation rates and intron 1 length, H3K36me3, and H3K4me1 can be explained almost entirely by exon density alone.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 presents results from iterative regression analysis showing these features don't correlate with residuals after accounting for exon density. This is an appropriate statistical approach for identifying independent vs dependent predictors. The analysis supports the conclusion that these features don't have independent effects beyond their correlation with exon density.

results.result: H3K79me2 and CpG content have independent components from each other, while CpG methylation is tightly associated with CpG content.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 present results from iterative regression analysis establishing relationships between predictors. The statistical approach is appropriate for identifying independent vs correlated features. The finding that methylation is tightly linked to CpG content is expected, while the independence of H3K79me2 and CpG content is informative for understanding their separate contributions.

results.result: Discussion of pausing regulation, stability, and the role of various factors in determining pausing dynamics and gene expression.
results.evaluation: These claims (C109, C117, C118, C122) represent discussion and interpretation of the results in context of the literature. C109 appropriately summarizes the main finding about universal P-TEFb dependence. C117 offers a reasonable model for pausing function. C118 and C122 cite relevant literature. These represent appropriate interpretation and contextualization of the findings.
